lessons.title: Why registration is the whole ballgame
lessons.hook: Before a single trade, rating, or advice note, one question decides whether you exist in GIFT-IFSC at all: are you registered as a Capital Market Intermediary? Get the gate wrong and everything downstream is unauthorised. This module is that gate.
lessons.cards: Eleven activities, one certificate each: LAW A unit in IFSC desirous of undertaking any of the listed activities shall obtain a certificate of registration from the Authority (Reg 4(1)). | PLAIN If your activity is on the Reg 4 list, you cannot operate without an IFSCA certificate. If it is not on the list, these regulations do not gate it. | WATCH The list is exhaustive. Don't assume a hybrid service is exempt — map it to the nearest listed activity first. || Unified registration (since 12 Jan 2026): LAW Proviso to Reg 4(1): a unit undertaking multiple activities may obtain a unified registration, in such manner as may be specified. | PLAIN A multi-desk unit can now hold one unified registration instead of collecting a separate certificate per activity. | WATCH Unified registration is NOT unified compliance — each activity still carries its own Chapter IV obligations and its own Part B conduct code. || Company/LLP/body corporate/branch — perpetual: LAW Reg 6: a CMI must be present in IFSC as a company, LLP, body corporate, or branch thereof. Reg 13: the certificate is perpetual unless suspended or cancelled. | PLAIN You need a recognised legal vehicle in the IFSC, and once granted, registration does not lapse on a renewal cycle. | WATCH 'Perpetual' surprises those used to periodic renewals elsewhere — there is no validity expiry to diarise, only suspension/cancellation risk.
lessons.summary: Reg 4 lists eleven registrable activities, each needing an IFSCA certificate; since 12 Jan 2026 a multi-activity unit may hold one unified registration; the vehicle must be a company/LLP/body corporate/branch (Reg 6); and the certificate is perpetual unless suspended or cancelled (Reg 13).
lessons.tip: Build an activity-to-obligation matrix on day one: list each activity the unit performs, the certificate that covers it, and the Chapter IV + Part B obligations it drags along. Unified registration makes this matrix more important, not less.

lessons.concept: Net worth: at all times, highest-not-sum, branch
lessons.title: Net worth: the number inspectors check first
lessons.hook: Net worth is the CMI's licence to keep operating. It is not a one-time entry figure — it must hold at all times. And the CMI framework has three quirks that trip up practitioners from a SEBI or RBI background: a liquid-assets definition for three categories, a highest-not-sum rule for multi-desk units, and no deposit at all.
lessons.cards: A continuing test, not an entry gate: LAW Reg 7(1): an entity shall comply with the net worth requirements in Schedule I, which shall be maintained at all times. | PLAIN Meeting the minimum on application day is not enough; you must stay above it continuously and be able to evidence it. | WATCH A quarterly statement of net worth is a mandatory record (Reg 16(1)(d)) — inspectors reconcile it against Schedule I. || Three categories measure differently: LAW Proviso to Reg 3(1)(cc): for a broker dealer, clearing member or investment banker, 'net worth' means the aggregate value of liquid assets (cash, bank balance, fixed deposits, Government Securities and other specified instruments). | PLAIN These three cannot count illiquid balance-sheet items toward net worth — only liquid assets qualify. | WATCH Everyone else uses the ordinary balance-sheet definition. Applying the wrong definition is a common, material error. || Multi-category units: LAW Reg 7(4): where an entity operates in multiple categories, it shall maintain the highest of the applicable minimum net worth requirements, unless otherwise specified. | PLAIN A unit doing three activities holds the single highest minimum among them — not the sum, not an average. | WATCH Do not add the category minimums together; and it is separate from and additional to net worth required for other (non-CMI) activities (Reg 7(3)).
lessons.summary: Schedule I sets each category's minimum; Reg 7(1) makes it a continuous 'at all times' test; three categories (broker dealer, clearing member, investment banker) measure net worth as liquid assets only (Reg 3(1)(cc) proviso); a multi-category unit holds the highest applicable minimum, not the sum (Reg 7(4)); and there is no deposit requirement anywhere.
lessons.tip: Maintain a live net-worth monitor, not a quarter-end scramble. For any unit with a broker-dealer, clearing-member or investment-banker desk, run a parallel liquid-assets computation — the balance-sheet figure can look healthy while the liquid-assets figure breaches.

lessons.module_name: Fit & Proper, Principal Officer & Compliance Officer
lessons.effective: experience route eased to 5 years w.e.f. 12 Jan 2026
lessons.title: The people tests behind every registration
lessons.hook: A CMI is only as registrable as its people. Two engines run here: the fit-and-proper test (applied to the entity and its key persons at all times) and the mandatory appointment of a Principal Officer and a separate Compliance Officer, both based in the IFSC.
lessons.cards: A continuous character test: LAW Reg 8(1): a CMI shall ensure that the entity and its principal officer, directors/designated partners, key managerial personnel and controlling shareholders are fit and proper persons, at all times. | PLAIN Fairness, integrity, honesty and good reputation — tested not just at entry but continuously, across a defined list of persons. | WATCH A disqualifying event (conviction for moral turpitude/economic offence, pending charge sheet, wilful defaulter, fugitive economic offender, etc.) can taint registration mid-life. || Principal Officer AND a separate Compliance Officer: LAW Reg 9(1): a CMI shall designate a principal officer and a separate compliance officer based out of IFSC. | PLAIN These are two distinct designated roles — you cannot collapse them into one person — and both must be located in the IFSC. | WATCH 'Separate' and 'based out of IFSC' are both hard requirements; a shared or offshore officer is a defect. || Education or experience gateway: LAW Reg 9(2): the PO and CO must meet specified educational qualifications (professional qualification or PG degree/diploma in finance, law, accountancy, management, commerce, economics, capital market, banking, insurance, actuarial science, fintech, science, technology, engineering or mathematics; or a graduate with five years' financial-services experience; CA/CS/CMA membership qualifies). | PLAIN There is a defined qualification-or-experience gateway; a law graduate is expressly eligible to be Compliance Officer. | WATCH The 'graduate + experience' route was amended to five years (from ten) w.e.f. 12 Jan 2026.
lessons.summary: Reg 8 makes fit-and-proper a continuous test across the entity and its key persons; Reg 9 requires a Principal Officer and a separate Compliance Officer, both based in the IFSC, meeting a defined qualification-or-experience gateway (graduate-plus-experience route eased to five years in 2026).
lessons.tip: Run fit-and-proper as an ongoing register, not an onboarding checkbox — capture directors, KMP and controlling shareholders, and re-test on any triggering event. Diarise PO/CO qualification evidence; at inspection, 'separate' and 'IFSC-based' are the first two boxes checked.

lessons.title: The conduct spine every CMI shares
lessons.hook: Whatever your category, one code binds you: Schedule II Part A. Reg 15 makes it mandatory for every CMI. This is the clearest 'common' layer in the whole regulation — and knowing it cold is what lets you separate shared duties from category-specific ones later.
lessons.cards: Reg 15 imports the whole code: LAW Reg 15: a CMI shall abide by the Code of Conduct as specified in Schedule II. | PLAIN The code is not optional guidance — it is a binding regulatory obligation for every CMI, enforceable like any other provision. | WATCH Schedule II has two parts: Part A binds all CMIs; Part B adds category-specific codes. Don't stop at Part A for a specific desk. || No manipulation, no false market: LAW Part A cl. 4-5: a CMI shall not indulge in manipulative, fraudulent or deceptive transactions/schemes or spread rumours to distort the market, nor create a false market singly or in collusion. | PLAIN Core market-integrity duties apply to everyone, not just trading desks. | WATCH 'Singly or in collusion' — participation in someone else's manipulation counts. || Confidentiality, conflicts, no exaggeration: LAW Part A cl. 7-9: no exaggerated claims about capability/qualifications; maintain client confidentiality except where law requires disclosure; avoid conflicts of interest, disclose them, and have a mechanism to resolve them. | PLAIN A baseline of honesty, confidentiality and conflict-management every CMI owes its clients. | WATCH Confidentiality yields only to a legal disclosure obligation — not to commercial convenience.
lessons.summary: Reg 15 imports Schedule II as a binding code; Part A binds every CMI (integrity, no manipulation, no false market, no exaggerated claims, confidentiality, conflict-management, prompt grievance handling, non-discrimination, prompt disclosure of material changes); Part B then layers category-specific codes on top.
lessons.tip: Treat Part A as the unit-wide conduct baseline and Part B as the desk overlay. When mapping obligations, tag each conduct duty 'A' (all CMIs) or 'B' (this category) — that tagging is exactly what the capstone tests.

lessons.title: The always-on obligations between inspections
lessons.hook: Registration is the gate; Chapter III is the daily discipline. Records, information duties, grievances, dispute resolution, business continuity, cyber, risk, change-in-control, fees and the annual compliance audit — this is the machinery an inspector expects to find running.
lessons.cards: Eight years, electronically retrievable: LAW Reg 16(1): a CMI shall maintain and preserve specified books, records and documents in electronic retrieval form for a minimum of eight years — including a quarterly statement of net worth and AML/CFT/KYC compliance documentation. | PLAIN A defined record set, kept retrievable for eight years, is mandatory — and it explicitly includes your quarterly net-worth evidence. | WATCH 'Electronic retrieval form' and 'eight years' are both hard minimums. || 15 days for officer changes; prior approval for control: LAW Reg 17(2): intimate any change in PO, CO or KMP within 15 days. Reg 23: a branch intimates a change in control within 15 days; an IFSC-incorporated CMI needs PRIOR approval of the Authority for a change in control. | PLAIN Different triggers, different clocks — and a branch merely notifies control changes, while an incorporated CMI must seek prior approval. | WATCH Confusing 'intimate within 15 days' with 'seek prior approval' is a classic error. || BCP, cyber, risk — and a 30 September audit: LAW Reg 20-22: maintain a BCP (annually reviewed), a cyber security/resilience framework, and risk-management/internal controls. Reg 25: an annual compliance audit by a CA/CS/CMA member (or foreign-authorised auditor), furnished to the Authority by 30 September. | PLAIN A resilience stack plus an independent annual compliance audit with a fixed filing date. | WATCH The audit report deadline is 30 September of the year — diarise it.
lessons.summary: Chapter III is the continuous-compliance engine: eight-year electronically-retrievable records (incl. quarterly net worth); 15-day intimation of PO/CO/KMP changes; BCP with annual review; cyber and risk frameworks; change-in-control (branch intimates in 15 days, incorporated CMI needs prior approval); fees; and an annual compliance audit filed by 30 September.
lessons.tip: Keep a compliance calendar keyed to these clocks — 15-day intimations, annual BCP review, 30 September audit filing — and a control log for change-in-control that distinguishes branch (notify) from incorporated (pre-approve). Inspectors test the machinery, not intentions.

lessons.title: What happens when the Authority looks — and acts
lessons.hook: Registration comes with a standing exposure to inspection and, if things go wrong, enforcement. Chapter V sets who can inspect and how; Chapter VI sets the consequence architecture. Knowing the shape of both turns an inspection from an ambush into a managed process.
lessons.cards: Suo motu, usually on notice: LAW Reg 37: the Authority may, suo motu or on information/complaint, appoint an inspecting authority to inspect a CMI's books, systems and procedures; notice is given, but may be dispensed with for reasons recorded in writing where investors' interest requires. | PLAIN Inspection can be triggered proactively; you will normally get notice, but not always. | WATCH Exchanges/CCs/depositories may separately inspect BD/CM/DP under their bye-laws; joint inspections are possible. || Suspension or cancellation grounds: LAW Reg 41: the Authority may suspend or cancel registration (or take other action) for failures such as breaching conditions, contravening the Act/regulations, furnishing false or misleading information, non-cooperation in inspection, or failing to resolve investor complaints. | PLAIN A defined set of grounds can cost you your registration. | WATCH 'Furnishing false or misleading information in any material particular' is its own standalone ground — accuracy to the Authority is not optional. || Relaxation and the power to be heard: LAW Reg 41 action follows process; Reg 44 lets the Authority relax strict enforcement on application with a non-refundable fee, processed within 30 days. Reg 47 repealed the 2021 CMI Regulations. | PLAIN There is a relaxation mechanism, and enforcement is bounded by process; the 2025 regime replaced the 2021 one. | WATCH Relaxation is discretionary and fee-bearing — not a right.
lessons.summary: Chapter V empowers inspection (suo motu or on complaint, usually on notice, with a dual layer for BD/CM/DP via their market infrastructure institutions); Chapter VI sets enforcement — suspension/cancellation on defined grounds (Reg 41), a fee-bearing relaxation power processed in 30 days (Reg 44), and the repeal of the 2021 Regulations (Reg 47).
lessons.tip: Prepare an inspection-readiness pack mapped to Reg 37's purposes (records, compliance, internal controls, fitness, complaints). Because false/misleading information is a standalone Reg 41 ground, institute a single accountable sign-off for everything filed with the Authority.

lessons.title: Broker-dealers & clearing members: exchange-tethered
lessons.hook: These two categories are unusual: their net worth is set not by IFSCA but by the market infrastructure institution, and their day-to-day rulebook is the exchange's or clearing corporation's bye-laws. They also share the liquid-assets net-worth test — a detail that separates them from most other CMIs.
lessons.cards: Set by the exchange / clearing corporation: LAW Schedule I: broker dealer net worth is 'as specified by the recognised stock exchange'; clearing member net worth is 'as specified by the recognised clearing corporation'. | PLAIN You look to the exchange/CC rulebook for the number, not a fixed USD figure in Schedule I. | WATCH But the DEFINITION of net worth for both is liquid assets only (Reg 3(1)(cc) proviso). || Comply with the MII bye-laws: LAW Reg 26: a broker dealer complies with the recognised stock exchange's bye-laws/rules/regulations; a clearing member complies with the recognised clearing corporation's. | PLAIN Your primary operating rulebook is the MII's, layered on top of the CMI Regulations. | WATCH This is also why BD/CM face a dual-oversight layer at inspection and enforcement. || Act across roles without a fresh certificate: LAW Reg 5(4)-(5): with the relevant approval, a clearing member may act as a broker dealer, a broker dealer may act as a clearing member, and each may operate across multiple exchanges/CCs — without a separate certificate of registration. | PLAIN Approved role-crossing does not require a new registration, just the MII's approval. | WATCH 'Without a separate certificate' is the key phrase — approval, not re-registration.
lessons.summary: Broker-dealer and clearing-member net worth is set by the exchange/clearing corporation (not a fixed Schedule I figure), but measured as liquid assets only; their operating rulebook is the MII's bye-laws (Reg 26); and Reg 5(4)-(5) lets them cross roles or operate across multiple MIIs with approval, without a fresh certificate.
lessons.tip: For a broker-dealer or clearing-member desk, maintain the liquid-assets net-worth computation continuously and align internal limits to the MII's specified figure. Track approvals under Reg 5(4)-(5) as evidence that role-crossing is authorised.

lessons.title: Credit rating agencies: the rating lifecycle duties
lessons.hook: A CRA's registration comes with a USD 200,000 net worth and a set of duties built around the integrity of the rating itself — from the client agreement, through continuous monitoring, to the tightly controlled circumstances in which a rating may be withdrawn.
lessons.cards: USD 200,000: LAW Schedule I, S.No. 3: Credit Rating Agency net worth is USD 200,000 (ordinary balance-sheet definition). | PLAIN A fixed USD figure, measured on the standard net-worth definition (not liquid assets). | WATCH Don't apply the liquid-assets carve-out here — that's only BD/CM/IB. || Written agreement per client: LAW Reg 28(1): a CRA shall enter into a written agreement with each client whose securities it proposes to rate, setting out rights, liabilities and fees. | PLAIN Every rating relationship is documented up front, including the fee. | WATCH No agreement, no rating — the agreement is the foundation. || Continuous monitoring; constrained withdrawal: LAW Reg 28(4)-(5): a CRA shall continuously monitor and periodically review ratings unless withdrawn, and shall generally not withdraw a rating while the rated obligations remain outstanding (subject to specified exceptions). | PLAIN A rating is a living obligation — monitored over its life, not a one-off opinion. | WATCH Withdrawal while obligations are outstanding is the exception, not the norm.
lessons.summary: A CRA holds USD 200,000 net worth (standard definition), documents each rating relationship in a written agreement covering rights/liabilities/fees (Reg 28(1)), and treats a rating as a living obligation — continuously monitored and periodically reviewed, and generally not withdrawn while the rated obligations are outstanding (Reg 28(4)-(5)).
lessons.tip: Operationalise the 'living rating' duty: a monitoring calendar per outstanding rating, with periodic reviews logged. Because withdrawal is constrained, document the specific triggering exception whenever a rating is withdrawn.

lessons.effective: net worth USD 1m w.e.f. 12 Jan 2026; existing comply by 30 Jun 2026
lessons.title: Custodians: segregation is the whole job
lessons.hook: The 2026 amendment reset the custodian net worth to USD 1 million and gave existing custodians until 30 June 2026 to comply. The operating duties orbit one principle: rigorous segregation and protection of client assets and records.
lessons.cards: USD 1 million (with a transition): LAW Schedule I, S.No. 4: Custodian net worth is USD 1 million (substituted for 'as specified by the Authority' w.e.f. 12 Jan 2026); existing custodians comply by 30 June 2026. | PLAIN A newly fixed USD 1 million floor, with a dated transition for incumbents. | WATCH Two dates matter: the 12 Jan 2026 amendment and the 30 June 2026 compliance deadline. || Custody separated from everything else: LAW Reg 29(1): a custodian shall separate and segregate its custodian activities from all other activities. | PLAIN Custody is ring-fenced operationally from the entity's other business lines. | WATCH Commingling custody with other activities is the cardinal custodian sin. || Client agreement + anti-manipulation controls: LAW Reg 29(3)-(4): a custodian enters an agreement with each client detailing custody circumstances, and maintains adequate internal controls to prevent manipulation of records and to protect them from theft and natural hazard. | PLAIN Documented client terms plus hard controls over the integrity and safety of records. | WATCH Records protection covers both manipulation and physical loss.
lessons.summary: Custodian net worth is USD 1 million since the 2026 amendment (existing custodians comply by 30 June 2026); operationally the custodian must segregate custody from all other activities (Reg 29(1)), document custody terms with each client, and run controls that protect records from both manipulation and physical loss (Reg 29(3)-(4)).
lessons.tip: If the group runs a custody desk alongside other CMI activities, evidence the operational segregation explicitly — separate systems, access controls and reconciliations. Diarise the 30 June 2026 net-worth deadline for any pre-existing custodian.

lessons.concept: Debenture trustee: independence, reporting, nominee director
lessons.title: Debenture trustees: the debenture-holders' watchdog
lessons.hook: The debenture trustee carries the highest fixed net worth in Schedule I — USD 1.5 million — because it stands guard for debenture holders. Its duties are concrete and time-bound: an independent trust deed, periodic reporting, and hard-wired escalation on default.
lessons.cards: USD 1.5 million — the highest fixed figure: LAW Schedule I, S.No. 5: Debenture Trustee net worth is USD 1.5 million. | PLAIN The largest fixed Schedule I minimum, reflecting the trustee's fiduciary weight. | WATCH Higher than the custodian's USD 1 million. || No conflict; agreement before subscription: LAW Reg 30(1)-(2): a DT enters an agreement with the issuer before the subscription list opens, and shall not be appointed where it is an associate of the issuer or is likely to have a conflict of interest. | PLAIN Independence from the issuer is a precondition, locked in before the issue opens. | WATCH Associate status or likely conflict is disqualifying. || Reporting cadence and nominee director on default: LAW Reg 30(3): the DT calls for periodic reports within seven days of the relevant board meeting or within forty-five days of the quarter, whichever is earlier; and appoints a nominee director on the issuer's board on two consecutive interest defaults, or default in security creation, or default in redemption. | PLAIN A defined reporting clock and an automatic escalation lever protecting holders. | WATCH 'Two consecutive defaults' in interest is the specific nominee-director trigger.
lessons.summary: The debenture trustee holds USD 1.5 million net worth — the highest fixed figure — must be independent of the issuer (no associate/conflict) with the agreement in place before subscription opens, and runs a defined reporting cadence (7 days of the board meeting or 45 days of the quarter, whichever is earlier) with a nominee-director escalation on two consecutive interest defaults or default in security creation/redemption (Reg 30).
lessons.tip: Build the DT's calendar around the 7-day/45-day reporting rule and pre-agree the nominee-director mechanics in the trust deed so the escalation is executable the moment the default trigger is hit.

lessons.title: Depository participants: segregation and daily reconciliation
lessons.hook: A DP's net worth is set by the depository, and its duties are built around beneficial-owner segregation and a strict daily reconciliation discipline — the operational heartbeat of a depository participant.
lessons.cards: Set by the depository: LAW Schedule I, S.No. 6: Depository Participant net worth is 'as specified by the depository'. | PLAIN Look to the recognised depository for the figure, not a fixed Schedule I number. | WATCH Like BD/CM, the number lives in the MII rulebook — but the DP uses the ordinary net-worth definition, not liquid assets. || Separate accounts per beneficial owner: LAW Reg 31(2): a DP shall open separate accounts in the name of each beneficial owner and segregate each owner's securities — never mixed with other owners' or the participant's own securities. | PLAIN Every beneficial owner's holdings are individually accounted and never commingled. | WATCH Mixing client holdings with proprietary holdings is a core breach. || Daily reconciliation with the depository: LAW Reg 31(5): a DP shall reconcile its records with the depository on a daily basis; and, where records are electronic, maintain data-processing integrity at all times (31(4)). | PLAIN Reconciliation is a daily obligation, not periodic. | WATCH 'Daily' is the operative cadence — a weekly or monthly cycle is non-compliant.
lessons.summary: A DP's net worth is set by the depository (standard definition), it must open separate accounts per beneficial owner and never commingle holdings (Reg 31(2)), maintain data-processing integrity (31(4)), and reconcile its records with the depository on a daily basis (31(5)).
lessons.tip: Automate the daily reconciliation and exception-handling; the 'daily' cadence is the single most testable DP duty. Prove beneficial-owner segregation through per-owner account structures and periodic segregation audits.

lessons.provision: Reg 32, Sch I, Sch II Part B
lessons.title: Distributors: who you can distribute to, and how
lessons.hook: A distributor's USD 50,000 net worth is modest, but its rulebook is detailed on scope — which products, to which clients, in which jurisdictions — and on conduct, with an extensive Part B code targeting mis-selling and rebates.
lessons.cards: USD 50,000: LAW Schedule I, S.No. 7: Distributor net worth is USD 50,000 (ordinary definition). | PLAIN A low fixed floor, on the standard net-worth basis. | WATCH Low capital, high conduct scrutiny — the risk here is conduct, not capital. || Defined distribution permissions: LAW Reg 32(1): a distributor may distribute capital market products/services to clients in IFSC or foreign jurisdictions (from regulated entities in India/IFSC/specified jurisdictions), to sophisticated investors more broadly, and to clients in India from IFSC/specified-jurisdiction providers. | PLAIN Who you may distribute to depends on the client type and the provider's jurisdiction. | WATCH The permission set is specific — sophisticated-investor distribution is wider than retail. || No mis-selling, no rebates: LAW Schedule II Part B (distributor): avoid mis-selling; act in clients' best interests; disclose material information; abstain from attracting clients through rebate; segregate proprietary investments; ensure advertisements are accurate, true, fair and complete. | PLAIN A dense anti-mis-selling, anti-inducement conduct code sits on top of Part A. | WATCH Offering rebates to attract clients is expressly prohibited.
lessons.summary: A distributor holds USD 50,000 net worth; its distribution permissions are defined by client type and provider jurisdiction (Reg 32(1)); and its heavy Part B conduct code targets mis-selling, best-interest dealing, disclosure, the rebate prohibition, proprietary-investment segregation and truthful advertising.
lessons.tip: For a distribution desk, the compliance centre of gravity is conduct, not capital: build a client-classification and product-eligibility matrix aligned to Reg 32(1), and hard-code the no-rebate and advertising-standards rules into sales governance.

lessons.title: ERDPPs: the newest category, comply-or-explain conduct
lessons.hook: The ESG Ratings and Data Products Provider is the framework's newest category, with a USD 25,000 net worth and a code of conduct applied on a 'comply or explain' basis — a lighter-touch, disclosure-led model distinct from the CRA regime.
lessons.cards: USD 25,000: LAW Schedule I, S.No. 8: ERDPP net worth is USD 25,000 (ordinary definition). | PLAIN A low fixed floor, matching the adviser/research-entity tier. | WATCH Same figure as IA and RE — a common point of confusion in the capstone. || A disclosure-led conduct model: LAW Reg 33(3)-(4): an ERDPP shall adhere to its code of conduct on a 'comply or explain' basis and disclose its compliance with that code. | PLAIN Rather than rigid rules, the ERDPP either complies or publicly explains departures. | WATCH 'Comply or explain' is distinctive — this is not the CRA's prescriptive rating regime. || ESG products, not credit ratings: LAW The ERDPP deals in ESG ratings and data products, a separate category from credit rating agencies. | PLAIN Don't map CRA duties onto an ERDPP — they are different registrations with different codes. | WATCH Treating an ERDPP like a CRA is a category error.
lessons.summary: The ERDPP is the newest CMI category (USD 25,000 net worth), operating a 'comply or explain' code of conduct with disclosure of compliance (Reg 33) — a disclosure-led model distinct from the prescriptive CRA regime, and not to be conflated with credit rating.
lessons.tip: For an ERDPP, build the 'comply or explain' disclosure into a published statement and keep the reasoning trail for any explained departures. Resist importing CRA-style monitoring/withdrawal duties — they belong to a different category.

lessons.title: Investment advisers: fiduciary, fee-only, conflict-clean
lessons.hook: The investment adviser holds USD 25,000 net worth, but its defining features are duties, not capital: a fiduciary standard, a prohibition on third-party remuneration, and a 15-day restriction on trading against its own advice.
lessons.cards: Act in the client's interest, disclose conflicts: LAW Reg 34(3): an investment adviser shall act in a fiduciary capacity towards its clients and disclose all conflicts of interest as and when they arise. | PLAIN The adviser is legally bound to put the client first and surface conflicts continuously. | WATCH Fiduciary is a higher bar than mere fair dealing. || No consideration from anyone but the client: LAW Reg 34(4): an IA shall not receive remuneration or compensation in any form from any person other than the client being advised, in respect of the underlying products. | PLAIN No product commissions or third-party payments — the adviser is paid only by the advised client. | WATCH This is the sharpest line between an adviser and a distributor. || 15-day own-account restriction: LAW Reg 34(6): an IA shall not transact on its own account contrary to advice given to clients for 15 days from the advice (with a 24-hour-notice exception if its assessment genuinely changes). | PLAIN The adviser cannot trade against its own live advice within the window. | WATCH The exception requires a revised assessment communicated to the client at least 24 hours in advance.
lessons.summary: An investment adviser (USD 25,000) acts in a fiduciary capacity and discloses conflicts (Reg 34(3)); may be paid only by the client advised, never by third parties (Reg 34(4)); maintains arm's-length between advisory and other activities (34(5)); and must not trade on its own account contrary to its advice for 15 days, save a 24-hour-notice exception (34(6)).
lessons.tip: The IA/distributor boundary is the practical crux: if any part of the remuneration comes from the product provider, you are not advising within Reg 34(4). Police the 15-day own-account rule with a monitored restricted-list tied to advice dates.

lessons.title: Investment bankers: issue management, liquid-assets net worth
lessons.hook: The investment banker holds USD 100,000 net worth measured on the liquid-assets test — one of only three categories to do so — and its duties centre on issue management: documented mandates, demarcated lead responsibilities, and hard conflict limits where it is close to the issuer.
lessons.cards: USD 100,000 — liquid assets: LAW Schedule I, S.No. 10: Investment Banker net worth is USD 100,000; and per Reg 3(1)(cc), net worth for an investment banker means liquid assets. | PLAIN A fixed USD 100,000 floor, but measured only on liquid assets. | WATCH The liquid-assets test is shared with broker dealers and clearing members. || Agreement with the issuer; demarcated leads: LAW Reg 35(1)-(2): an IB enters an agreement with the issuer specifying its roles and responsibilities; where there are multiple lead investment bankers, each one's responsibilities are clearly demarcated. | PLAIN The engagement is documented, and in a syndicate each lead's remit is delineated. | WATCH Undemarcated lead responsibilities are a governance gap. || Promoter/associate → marketing only: LAW Reg 35(3): where the IB is a promoter or associate of the issuer (or of a person making an offer), it shall not undertake any activity except marketing of the issue/offer. | PLAIN Closeness to the issuer collapses the IB's permissible role down to marketing. | WATCH This is a bright-line conflict limit, not a disclosure-only duty.
lessons.summary: An investment banker (USD 100,000, liquid-assets net worth) documents its mandate with the issuer (Reg 35(1)), demarcates responsibilities among multiple lead bankers (35(2)), and — where it is a promoter or associate of the issuer — is confined to marketing the issue only (35(3)), with further limits on own-account/associate dealing (35(4)).
lessons.tip: For an IB desk, run the liquid-assets net-worth computation continuously (the balance-sheet figure is irrelevant to the floor), and screen every mandate for promoter/associate status with the issuer — if present, the role is marketing-only, full stop.

lessons.title: Research entities: independence, and the registration exemption
lessons.hook: The research entity holds USD 25,000 net worth, and its duties centre on the independence and integrity of research. Its most distinctive feature is a registration exemption: an already-registered IA, CRA or FME issuing research to the public need not separately register as a research entity.
lessons.cards: No separate registration if already IA/CRA/FME: LAW Reg 4(4): a person need not obtain separate registration as a 'Research Entity' if it is an investment adviser or credit rating agency or Fund Management Entity registered with the Authority that issues, circulates or distributes research reports to the public. | PLAIN Existing registrants issuing public research aren't forced into a second registration. | WATCH The exemption is specific to IA/CRA/FME registrants — not a blanket exemption. || Ring-fence research from other business: LAW Reg 36(4): a research entity shall have appropriate mechanisms to ensure the independence of its research activities from its other business activities. | PLAIN Research must be insulated from the pressures of the entity's other lines. | WATCH Independence is structural, not merely aspirational. || Control analyst dealing: LAW Reg 36(1),(5)-(6): written policies governing employee/analyst dealing and trading; personal trading of analysts monitored, recorded and, where necessary, subject to formal approval. | PLAIN Analyst personal trading is policed to protect research objectivity. | WATCH Monitoring plus, where needed, pre-approval — not an honour system.
lessons.summary: A research entity (USD 25,000) protects research integrity through structural independence from other business (Reg 36(4)) and controlled analyst personal trading (Reg 36(5)-(6)); and under Reg 4(4), an IA/CRA/FME already registered and issuing public research need not separately register as a research entity.
lessons.tip: Confirm at onboarding whether the research function even needs its own registration (the Reg 4(4) exemption may apply), then operationalise analyst personal-trading controls with monitoring and a pre-approval gate for sensitive trades.

lessons.title: Common or entity-specific? The practitioner's real test
lessons.hook: In a real compliance seat, the question is rarely 'what does the regulation say?' — it's 'does THIS obligation bind every CMI, or only this desk?' Confuse the two and you either over-comply (wasteful) or under-comply (dangerous). This capstone drills exactly that judgment across the whole regulation.
lessons.cards: What binds everyone: LAW Common Core: registration (Reg 4), net worth framework (Reg 7), fit-and-proper and PO/CO (Reg 8-9), Schedule II Part A conduct (Reg 15), governance & resilience (Reg 16-25), inspection & enforcement (Reg 37-47). | PLAIN These bind every CMI regardless of category — the shared spine. | WATCH Part A conduct and Chapter III obligations are common; don't mistake them for category quirks. || What is category-specific: LAW Category specifics: distinct net-worth figures (Schedule I), Chapter IV obligations (Reg 26-36) and Schedule II Part B codes — e.g., IA fee-only rule, DP daily reconciliation, DT nominee director, IB promoter-marketing limit, CRA rating monitoring. | PLAIN Each category drags along its own obligations that do NOT bind the others. | WATCH The liquid-assets net-worth definition is entity-specific (only BD/CM/IB). || Tag every obligation A or B: LAW For any obligation, ask: is it in the Common Core (binds all) or a Chapter IV / Part B / Schedule I category rule (binds one)? | PLAIN A simple, repeatable classification that prevents both over- and under-compliance. | WATCH Unified registration makes this tagging more important, not less.
lessons.summary: Every CMI obligation is either common (registration, net worth framework, fit-and-proper, Part A conduct, governance, inspection/enforcement) or entity-specific (category net-worth figures, Chapter IV duties, Part B codes). The practitioner's core skill is tagging each obligation correctly — especially in a multi-desk unit.
lessons.tip: Keep a two-column obligation register per unit: 'common (all desks)' and 'entity-specific (this desk)'. When a new obligation appears, classify it before you operationalise it — that single habit prevents the most common compliance errors in a multi-category CMI.
